verses.1: Woe to the land of swift wings across the rivers of Cush.
verses.2: The one who sends envoys by sea and sends scrolls on the water. For messengers will go light-footed to a distant people, to a nation terrifying and strange. Who is it beyond them? A nation of no hope and trampled down. Now the rivers of its land.
verses.3: All who dwell in the world and live on the earth, like lifting a signal on the hills you will see, like the sound of a trumpet you will hear.
verses.4: For thus the LORD said to me: I will keep quiet and watch my safe refuge, like the heat of midday, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest.
verses.5: Before the harvest, when the bloom is cut down, and the fruit-bearing branch is made barren, the reaper will cut off the tender clusters with the sickle, and the remaining tendrils he will cast away.
verses.6: They will be left together to the birds of the hills and to the beasts of the earth, and the vulture will settle on it, and all the beasts of the earth will mock it.
verses.7: In that time, tribute will be brought to the LORD of Hosts by a weary and crushed people, and from a nation terrible now and forever. A nation of hope and trampled down, which lies in the portion of the rivers of its land, to the place of the name of the LORD of Hosts, the mountain of Zion.

notes:
Notes
- v. 2: The phrase "scrolls on the water" reflects the Hebrew term for "writing on papyrus" (כְּלֵי־גֹמֶא) and its likely use here as a metaphor for messages sent via water-borne messengers.
- v. 5: "The reaper will cut off the tender clusters" reflects the metaphorical use of agricultural imagery to describe divine judgment.
- v. 7: "Tribute will be brought to the LORD of Hosts" is based on the context of a distant people bringing offerings to Zion, likely as a sign of submission and acknowledgment of divine authority.
raw:
[1] Woe to the land of swift wings across the rivers of Cush.

[2] The one who sends envoys by sea and sends scrolls on the water. For messengers will go light-footed to a distant people, to a nation terrifying and strange. Who is it beyond them? A nation of no hope and trampled down. Now the rivers of its land.

[3] All who dwell in the world and live on the earth, like lifting a signal on the hills you will see, like the sound of a trumpet you will hear.

[4] For thus the LORD said to me: I will keep quiet and watch my safe refuge, like the heat of midday, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest.

[5] Before the harvest, when the bloom is cut down, and the fruit-bearing branch is made barren, the reaper will cut off the tender clusters with the sickle, and the remaining tendrils he will cast away.

[6] They will be left together to the birds of the hills and to the beasts of the earth, and the vulture will settle on it, and all the beasts of the earth will mock it.

[7] In that time, tribute will be brought to the LORD of Hosts by a weary and crushed people, and from a nation terrible now and forever. A nation of hope and trampled down, which lies in the portion of the rivers of its land, to the place of the name of the LORD of Hosts, the mountain of Zion.

---
Notes
- v. 2: The phrase "scrolls on the water" reflects the Hebrew term for "writing on papyrus" (כְּלֵי־גֹמֶא) and its likely use here as a metaphor for messages sent via water-borne messengers.
- v. 5: "The reaper will cut off the tender clusters" reflects the metaphorical use of agricultural imagery to describe divine judgment.
- v. 7: "Tribute will be brought to the LORD of Hosts" is based on the context of a distant people bringing offerings to Zion, likely as a sign of submission and acknowledgment of divine authority.
